summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state, and Delta has no protective statute of its own.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on gatherings of LGBTQ+ people. In June 2018 police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court. In August 2023 police raided a gathering in Warri, and 67 people were charged to court.

The Warri raid is the most fully documented. Officers from the Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area arrested 67 suspects at 9 pm on 27 August 2023 at Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding between Daniel Pius, 22, described as the groom, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20, described as the bride. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the operation followed a confession by a person he described as a male cross-dresser, who said he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony. The suspects fled on the officers' arrival and 67 were chased and arrested. Drugs and what Edafe called gay marriage ceremonial dresses were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and that efforts to arrest those who fled would continue for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

A separate account of the same date records that police in Delta State raided a party organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 people, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account.

Victims of predatory same-sex assault in Delta under-report to police for fear of prosecution themselves, according to a human rights lawyer based in Warri.

Documentation of Delta-specific enforcement is thin, and thin documentation does not demonstrate safety.
tangentialFactors:
Delta enforcement actions are frequently reported alongside drug allegations, which widens the stated basis for arrest beyond the same-sex conduct allegation itself.

The August 2023 Warri raid is described in two ways. Police characterised it as a same-sex wedding; some civil society representatives disputed that and described a party organised by the LGBTQI+ community. The number held also differs between accounts, with 67 charged to court and more than 200 reported detained.

Venue-based enforcement in Delta spans at least five years, from the Asaba arrests of June 2018 to the Warri raid of August 2023.
localsOnly:
People arrested in Delta face court proceedings that can extend over years. The group arrested in Asaba in June 2018 was still facing homosexuality-related charges in court the following month, and the 67 charged after the August 2023 Warri raid were brought to court.

Police stated that efforts to arrest those who fled the August 2023 raid would continue for possible prosecution, leaving outstanding exposure for residents who left the scene.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the prosecutions arising from the August 2023 Warri raid is unresolved; sources show only that 67 people were charged to court.

The disposition of the Asaba case after July 2018 is not sourced.

Whether the August 2023 gathering was a wedding or a party is disputed and unresolved, as is the number held: 67 charged and more than 200 detained are both reported for the same date.

The allegation by one suspect that he was sexually assaulted at the hotel while intoxicated has no recorded follow-up, and no outcome is sourced for the drugs and ceremonial dresses recovered.
